topics.algebraicExpressions: Algebraic expressions in equations and graphs

sets.defineTitle: What is a set, and how do we give one?
sets.defineIntro1: Picture a box you put things into: numbers, shapes, people. The only rule is that for any thing it must be unambiguous whether it is inside. Here we choose from twelve elements.
sets.defineIntro2: There are two ways to give a set. By listing: name the elements it contains. By a rule: state a property, and everything satisfying it belongs. The two can describe the very same set, which you can try below.
sets.defineDef1: Set: a collection of things where, for any thing, it is unambiguous whether it belongs. The things that belong are the elements of the set, written x ∈ A.
sets.defineDef2: Universal set (U): the stock of things we choose the elements from.
sets.defineDef3: Empty set (∅): the set with no elements at all. The size of a set (|A|) is the number of its elements.
sets.defineRuleLabel: Given by a rule, the same set:
sets.defineNoRule: None of the offered rules fits this selection, so it can only be given by listing. That is perfectly fine: every finite set can be listed, but not every one has a short rule.
sets.defineCardinality: The size of the set is {{size}}. When nothing belongs we get the empty set, written ∅.
sets.defineTask: Click the elements for which this holds: divisible by 3 and greater than 6.
sets.defineHint: Both conditions must hold at once, so 3 and 6 do not qualify.
sets.relIntro1: Two sets can stand in one of five relations, and it is always the elements that decide, never the picture.
sets.relDef1: Subset: A is a subset of B (A ⊆ B) if every element of A is also an element of B. If B also has an element that A lacks, then A is a proper subset of B (A ⊂ B).
sets.relDef2: Equal sets: A = B when they have exactly the same elements. Disjoint sets: they share no element, that is A ∩ B = ∅.
sets.relIntro2: Pick two rules and watch which relation appears. The picture always follows what the elements say.
sets.rel_equal: A = B — the sets are equal, holding exactly the same elements.
sets.rel_subsetAB: A ⊆ B — every element of A is in B, but B has an element that A does not.
sets.rel_subsetBA: B ⊆ A — every element of B is in A, but A has an element that B does not.
sets.rel_disjoint: A ∩ B = ∅ — the sets are disjoint, sharing no element.
sets.rel_overlap: They share elements, but neither is a subset of the other.
sets.relTask: Set the two rules so that A is a proper subset of B: every element of A lies in B, and the two are not equal.
sets.relHint: Look for a property stricter than another. Whatever is divisible by 6 is also even.
sets.opsIntro1: Two or three sets cut the universe into regions on a Venn diagram. Each region says exactly which circles you are inside and which you are outside.
sets.opsIntro2: There are four basic operations, and each picks out a group of regions in the drawing. Choose an expression, or shade freely and see what the result is called.
sets.opsDef1: Union (A ∪ B): the elements that are in A or in B, that is in at least one of them.
sets.opsDef2: Intersection (A ∩ B): the elements that are in A and in B.
sets.opsDef3: Difference (A ∖ B): the elements that are in A but not in B.
sets.opsDef4: Complement (Ā): the elements of the universal set that are not in A.
sets.opsNoName: This shading has no simple name among the ones listed. Every set of regions can be described, but not all of them have a short form.
sets.opsTask: Shade the region this expression denotes. Click the diagram or use the buttons.
sets.opsHint: Shade only what lies in A but in neither B nor C.
sets.logicIntro1: Set operations and logical operations are the same thing in different words. An element is in A ∩ B when it is in A and in B. It is in A ∪ B when it is in A or in B.
sets.logicIntro2: Every row of the truth table is exactly one Venn region. Hover a row or a region and watch its partner light up.
sets.logicRowHint: Each row of the table is one region of the diagram.
sets.logicDeMorganSame: The two shadings are identical. That is De Morgan's law: whatever is not in both A and B is left out of A or left out of B.
sets.logicTask: Which expression describes the shaded region?
sets.logicHint: It is the shared part that is left out. That makes it the complement of the intersection.
sets.logicRegionsHint: The shading covers {{regions}} of the four regions.
sets.countIntro1: To say how many elements are in A ∪ B, the obvious move is to add |A| and |B|. But that counts the shared part twice, since it lies in both sets.
sets.countIntro2: The repair is simple: subtract the intersection once. This is the sieve. Drag the slider and watch the × marks in the regions, because every region must finish at exactly ×1.
sets.countStep0: Start from nothing. Drag the slider right and the sieve builds up one step at a time.
sets.countStepMid: Look at the × marks: overlapping regions have now been counted more than once. The next step corrects that.
sets.countStepDone: Every region reads ×1. That is exactly why the sieve works: after the alternating sum, each element has been counted precisely once.
sets.countEqual: The two agree, as they must: the sieve gives the same answer as simply adding up the regions.
sets.countTask: A class has {{all}} students. Of them {{foot}} play football, {{swim}} swim, and {{both}} do both. How many do neither?
sets.countHint: First work out how many do at least one sport, then subtract from the class size.
sets.partIntro1: To classify is to sort: by shape, by colour, by remainder. We demand two things: nothing lands in two places, and nothing is left out.
sets.partDef: Classification (partition): splitting a set into subsets that are pairwise disjoint and together cover the whole set. Every element then lands in exactly one class.
sets.partIntro2: Pick a criterion. The third one is deliberately wrong, so look at what breaks, because a failed example is what really shows the definition its teeth.
sets.partIsPartition: This is a classification: every element landed in exactly one class.
sets.partBadOverlap_one: Not a classification: {{count}} element belongs to two classes at once ({{list}}).
sets.partBadOverlap_other: Not a classification: {{count}} elements belong to two classes at once ({{list}}).
sets.partBadGap_one: On top of that, {{count}} element landed in no class at all ({{list}}).
sets.partBadGap_other: On top of that, {{count}} elements landed in no class at all ({{list}}).
sets.partPool: Choose the active class, then click the elements that belong there.
sets.partTask: Place all twelve elements according to their remainder mod 3.
sets.partHint: The remainder is 0, 1 or 2. Twelve, for instance, divides by three exactly.
sets.infTitle: Infinite sets: as many, or fewer?
sets.infIntro1: For finite sets it goes without saying that a proper subset has fewer elements. Pick the girls out of a class of ten and there will certainly be fewer than ten.
sets.infDef: Same cardinality: two sets are the same size when their elements can be paired up with nothing left over: every element has exactly one partner in the other set, and nothing is left out on either side.
sets.infIntro2: For infinite sets this breaks down. Look: every positive integer has exactly one even partner, and the other way round too. Nothing is left out on either side.
sets.infParadox: The even numbers form a proper subset of the positive integers, and yet there are exactly as many of them. Switch on the true number line: the arrows fan out and the evens look sparser, but still not one number is left out.
sets.infTask: Under the pairing n ↦ 3n, which number is the partner of 7?

venn.ariaDeMorganLeft: Venn diagram: complement of A intersect B
venn.ariaDeMorganRight: Venn diagram: union of the complements of A and B

logic.stmtIntro1: Mathematical logic works with statements: sentences that can be judged true or not. There is no third option: a statement is either true or false.
logic.stmtIntro2: Not every sentence is a statement. Questions, commands and exclamations are not, because they have no truth value: "What time is it?" is neither true nor false. A false statement is still a statement.
logic.stmtDef: Statement: a declarative sentence that is unambiguously either true or false. These two options are the truth value of the statement.
logic.stmtOpen: The trap is the open sentence: "x + 2 = 5" is not a statement on its own, because its truth value depends on what we put in place of x. With x = 3 it is true, with x = 4 it is false. It becomes a statement once x is fixed, or once we say "for every x" or "there is an x".
logic.stmtOpenDef: Open sentence: a sentence containing an unknown, so its truth value depends on what we put in place of the unknown. For example "x + 2 = 5".
logic.stmtTask: Decide for each sentence: a true statement, a false statement, or not a statement at all?
logic.stmtHint: Questions and commands have no truth value. An equation with an unknown is an open sentence: its value depends on the unknown.
logic.sentAngles: The interior angles of a triangle add up to 200°.
logic.negIntro1: Every statement has a twin that says the exact opposite. Exactly one of the two is always true: when one is true, the other is false, and the other way round.
logic.negIntro2: In the language of sets, negation is the complement: if the truth set of P is A, the truth set of ¬P is everything outside A. Negating twice gives the original back: ¬¬P = P.
logic.negDef: Negation: the negation of a statement P (¬P, read "not P") is the statement that is true exactly when P is false.
logic.negSentence2: ¬¬P: it is not true that the element is not {{p}}, that is, the element is {{p}}.
logic.negCount: The statement is true for {{n}} elements and false for the remaining {{rest}}. For any element, either the statement or its negation is true: never both, never neither.
logic.negPairsTitle: Common negations, and the common mistake
logic.negPair_and_s: It is raining and the wind is blowing.
logic.negPair_and_w: It is not raining and the wind is not blowing.
logic.negPair_and_r: It is not raining or the wind is not blowing.
logic.negPair_all_r: There is a student who did not bring their book.
logic.negPair_some_s: There is a number that is negative.
logic.negPair_some_w: There is a number that is not negative.
logic.negTask: What is the negation of "The number is greater than 6."? Pick one, then compare the two selections: the negation must select exactly the elements the original left out.
logic.negHint: The negation of "greater than 6" must include 6 itself, since 6 is not greater than 6.
logic.negChoiceNotGt7: The number is not greater than 7.
logic.negChoiceLt7: The number is less than 7 but not 6.
logic.negTaskOriginal: The original statement is true for these elements:
logic.connIntro1: Two statements can be joined into a new one. The connecting word decides when the new statement is true, and here mathematics is more precise than everyday language.
logic.connDef1: And (A ∧ B): true when both A and B are true.
logic.connDef2: Or (A ∨ B), the inclusive or: true when at least one is true; both being true is fine too.
logic.connDef3: Exclusive or (A ⊕ B): true when exactly one of the two is true.
logic.connIntro2: Everyday "or" often means something else: "either tea or coffee" means one of the two, not both. That is the exclusive or. In mathematics a plain "or" is always the inclusive one: both being true is fine too.
logic.connSentence_xor: The element is either {{a}} or {{b}} (but not both).
logic.vennConnAria: Venn diagram: the elements with properties A and B, the result of the connective shaded
logic.connRowHint: Each row of the table is one region of the diagram. Hover over a row!
logic.connSetLink: Sets and logic are the same thing in two languages. "And" is the intersection, "or" is the union, and exclusive or is the union of the two differences. "x ∈ A ∩ B" says precisely "x ∈ A and x ∈ B".
logic.connResult: The compound statement is true for these elements: {{list}}.
logic.connTask: Select the elements that are either even or divisible by 3, in the exclusive sense!
logic.connHint: 6 and 12 are both even and divisible by 3. The exclusive or rules out exactly those.
logic.quantIntro1: The words "for all" and "there is" turn an open sentence into a statement: "x is even" is neither true nor false on its own, but "every element is even" can be judged.
logic.quantDef1: For all (∀): "every element …" is true when there is not a single exception. There is (∃): "there is an element that …" is true when at least one such element exists.
logic.quantDef2: Counterexample: a single case for which a "for all" statement fails. One counterexample brings the whole statement down.
logic.quantIntro2: This makes them asymmetric: a "for all" statement is refuted by a single counterexample, and a "there is" statement is confirmed by a single example. To confirm a "for all" statement, though, you must check every case (or prove it, see section 7).
logic.quantNoWitness: There is not a single example.
logic.quantNegSentence_all: Negation: There is an {{d}} that is not {{p}}. →
logic.quantNegNote: Notice that of the statement and its negation, exactly one is true. The negation of "every element is even" is not "no element is even" but "there is an element that is not even".
logic.quantTask: "Every element greater than 6 is even." This statement is false. Mark a counterexample!
logic.quantHint: A counterexample is an element that is greater than 6 but not even.
logic.impIntro1: An "if…, then…" statement is a promise: when the premise holds, the conclusion has to hold too. The promise can be broken in only one way: the premise happens and the conclusion does not.
logic.impIntro2: This can be surprising: when the premise is false, the statement is automatically true, whatever the conclusion. "If 5 is even, then the Moon is made of cheese" is true, because the promise never had to be kept. "If…, then…" says nothing about the case where the premise fails.
logic.impDef: Implication ("if P, then Q", P ⇒ Q): P is the premise, Q the conclusion. The statement is false only when P is true but Q is false; in every other case it is true.
logic.impSentence: If an element is {{p}}, then it is {{q}}. →
logic.impCounter: Counterexample: {{list}}. For these the premise is true and the conclusion false.
logic.vennImpAria: Venn diagram: the elements with properties P and Q, the counterexample region shaded
logic.impRowHint: The shaded region is the only one where the statement can fail: P true, Q false. Hover over a row!
logic.impSetLink: With sets: "if P, then Q" means precisely that the truth set of P is a subset of the truth set of Q. If the shaded region is empty, A ⊆ B.
logic.impConverseIntro: Premise and conclusion can swap places, but that does not give the same statement. In the example below one is true and the other false.
logic.impConverseDef: Converse: the converse of "if P, then Q" is "if Q, then P". It is a separate statement whose truth value may differ from the original. Contrapositive: "if not Q, then not P". It always says the same as the original.
logic.impConverseSentence: Converse: If an element is {{q}}, then it is {{p}}. →
logic.impContraSentence: If an element is not {{q}}, then it is not {{p}}. →
logic.impContraNote: The last one is the contrapositive: negate both sides and swap. It always says the same as the original; try any setting. That is why an "if…, then…" statement can be proved by proving its contrapositive.
logic.impTask: Given the statement "If a number is divisible by 6, then it is even." Pick its converse, then decide whether the converse is true or false!
logic.impHint: In the converse, premise and conclusion swap without negation. Then look for an even number that is not divisible by 6.
logic.impChoice_converse: If a number is even, then it is divisible by 6.
logic.impChoice_inverse: If a number is not divisible by 6, then it is not even.
logic.impChoice_contrapositive: If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 6.
logic.iffIntro1: "If and only if" is two "if…, then…" statements at once: there and back. It is true when both directions are true, and false when either direction has a counterexample.
logic.iffIntro2: With sets: the two truth sets are equal. That is why "if and only if" statements are the definitions and characterisations of mathematics: two different wordings that describe exactly the same things.
logic.iffDef: Equivalence ("P if and only if Q", P ⇔ Q): means both P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P at once. It is true when P and Q have the same truth value.
logic.vennIffAria: Venn diagram: the elements with properties P and Q, the two difference regions shaded
logic.iffSentence: An element is {{p}} if and only if it is {{q}}. →
logic.iffSame: The two properties pick out exactly the same elements; the shaded region is empty.
logic.iffDiffer: There are elements in the shaded region, so the two properties do not pick out the same elements.
logic.iffSetLink: With sets: "P if and only if Q" means precisely that the two truth sets are equal: neither sticks out of the other.
logic.iffTask: Find two differently worded properties for which the "if and only if" statement is true!
logic.iffHint: Look for a pair with no counterexample in either direction. One property is compound and the other simple, yet they pick out the same elements.
logic.proofIntro1: In mathematics it is not enough that something works many times over: it has to be proved. A proof is not a collection of examples but an argument after which the statement is certainly true in every case.
logic.proofIntro2: Refuting is cheap by comparison: to bring down a "for all" statement, a single counterexample is enough. So in mathematics, checking a thousand cases is not enough, but finding one bad case is.
logic.proofDef: Theorem: a statement that has been proved. Proof: an argument that derives the statement from known truths by logical steps and covers all cases at once.
logic.proofEulerIntro: Look at the expression below: substituting n = 0, 1, 2, … gives prime numbers. For how long? Step through the cases!
logic.proofStripAria: Values of n² + n + 41 for n from 0 to 44, primes in green, composite numbers in red
logic.proofNotPrime: n = {{n}}: {{value}} is not prime, because it is {{a}} · {{b}}.
logic.proofEulerMoral: The first {{first}} cases all give primes, and yet at n = {{first}} the claim fails. No number of examples is a proof, but a single counterexample is a refutation.
logic.proofCourt1: Imagine a trial where the statement is the defendant. The prosecutor has it easy: showing a single counterexample is enough, and the statement falls. The defence has it harder: examples do not count, because the prosecutor can always ask, "and what about the other cases?".
logic.proofCourt2: The defence has one weapon: a proof, an argument that covers every case at once, for instance by calculating with letters that can stand for any number. In the task below you put the steps of such a proof in order.
logic.proofTask: Theorem: the sum of two odd numbers is even. The steps below are the sentences of the proof, shuffled. Click them in the right order!
logic.proofHint: First name the things you are talking about; at the end, say why what you got is even.
logic.proofStep_name: Let the two odd numbers be 2k + 1 and 2m + 1, where k and m are integers.
logic.proofStep_conclude: k + m + 1 is an integer, so the sum is an integer multiple of 2, hence even.
logic.gamesIntro: Logic is not only for theorems. Two classic games follow: in one, "true or false" decides who is who; in the other, a simple "if…, then…" rule wins every round.
logic.islandIntro1: Two kinds of people live on an island: knights always tell the truth, knaves always lie. They look alike. We meet two islanders, Anna and Ben; we do not know which is which, we only hear what they say.
logic.islandIntro2: The method: go through all four possibilities for who is who. Each assumption is one row of the table. Under that assumption, check whether what the speaker said is true, and whether by their kind they should be telling the truth. Where the two disagree, that assumption is a contradiction and is out. What remains is the solution.
logic.sayDifferent: "The two of us are of different kinds."
logic.sayAtLeastOneKnave: "At least one of us is a knave."
logic.islandColShould: By {{name}}'s kind, should it be true?
logic.islandWorkedMoral: Only one assumption survives: Anna is a knave, Ben is a knight. A knight can never call herself a knave, and a knave's sentence must be false, so Ben has to be a knight.
logic.islandTask: Pick a puzzle and decide from the sentences who is a knight and who is a knave! The same two islanders speak: Anna and Ben.
logic.islandHint: Go through all four cases. A sentence "fits" when a knight says something true or a knave says something false.
logic.islandManySolutions_other: This puzzle has {{count}} solutions: the sentences do not settle who is who. Either answer is correct.
logic.nimTitle: NIM: who takes the last match?
logic.nimIntro1: From a pile of matches, players alternately take 1, 2 or 3. Whoever takes the last match wins. You start, the computer replies. Try to beat it, then turn on the hint and see the secret!
logic.nimYouWin: You took the last one. You win!
logic.nimCpuWins: The computer took the last one. Turn on the hint and see where the game slipped away!
logic.nimHintLosing: The pile is a multiple of 4: there is no winning move from here unless the computer slips.
logic.nimHintTake_one: Winning move: take {{count}} so that {{left}} remain.
logic.nimHintTake_other: Winning move: take {{count}} so that {{left}} remain.
logic.nimStrategy: The strategy: if you leave your opponent a multiple of 4, whatever they take (1, 2 or 3) you can top it up to 4, and at the end the move 4 → 0 is yours. In other words: if the pile is not a multiple of 4, then the player to move can win. {{losing}}
logic.nimStartLosing: The current starting pile is a multiple of 4, so as the first player you can only win if the computer slips, and it will not. Pick another size!
logic.nimStartWinning: The current starting pile is not a multiple of 4, so as the first player you can win if you choose every move well.

combi.prodIntro1: In the morning you pick one of 2 t-shirts and one of 3 pairs of trousers. How many outfits are there? Let us draw it. The first branching decides the t-shirt, the second the trousers, and the leaves of the tree are the finished outfits: 2 · 3 = 6.
combi.prodIntro2: The picture also shows when multiplying is allowed: every t-shirt has the same number of trousers hanging off it. If one step had more options after some earlier choices than after others, the branches would not look alike and multiplying would break.
combi.prodTreeAria: Choice tree with {{steps}} steps and {{total}} possibilities.
combi.prodTooMany: That is too many branches to draw: {{total}} possibilities. Remove a step or pick fewer options.
combi.prodLeaves: The number of leaves is the number of possibilities: {{total}}.
combi.prodRule: Multiplication rule: if a choice is made in several steps, and every step has the same number of options no matter what was chosen before, then the number of possibilities is the product of the options of the steps.
combi.prodTask: The canteen offers 3 soups, 4 main courses and 2 desserts. How many different lunches can you put together if you take exactly one of each?
combi.prodHint: Three steps one after the other, and none of them affects the others: multiply.
combi.sumTitle: 2. Case separation: when do we add?
combi.sumIntro1: The snack bar has 4 sandwiches and 3 pastries. If you buy one thing, you have 4 + 3 = 7 choices: either a sandwich, or a pastry. The two cases never mix, so we add them up.
combi.sumIntro2: But if you buy a sandwich and a drink, and there are 5 drinks, the two decisions come one after the other: 4 · 5 = 20 possibilities. In short: "or" adds, "and" multiplies.
combi.sumAria_or: {{a}} dots in the first row and {{b}} dots in the second, {{total}} dots in total.
combi.sumAria_and: A grid of dots with {{b}} rows and {{a}} columns, {{total}} dots in total.
combi.sumRead_or: You pick a single thing from one of the two groups: {{a}} + {{b}} = {{total}} possibilities.
combi.sumRead_and: You pick one from each group, and every dot is one pair: {{a}} · {{b}} = {{total}} possibilities.
combi.sumRule: Addition rule: if you split the possibilities into cases that exclude each other, you add up the sizes of the cases. This is case separation: you cut a hard problem into a few easier ones.
combi.sumExprTask: Which story does this expression belong to?
combi.sumExprHint: The product stands for two decisions one after the other, while the + sign separates two different cases.
combi.exprOrDress: I pick one of the 4 t-shirts and one of the 3 pairs of trousers, or I put on one of my 5 dresses.
combi.exprAllThree: I put on one of the 4 t-shirts, one of the 3 pairs of trousers and one of the 5 pairs of shoes.
combi.exprOnlyOne: I put on a single item of clothing: one of the 4 t-shirts, the 3 pairs of trousers or the 5 dresses.
combi.wrongProblem: Problem: how many two-digit numbers can be made from the digits 1, 2, 3 if the two digits must be different?
combi.wrongStep1: The first digit can be chosen in 3 ways.
combi.wrongStep2: The second digit can also be chosen in 3 ways.
combi.wrongTask: One step of this solution is wrong. Which one?
combi.wrongHint: Write out all the numbers: 12, 13, 21, 23, 31, 32. Then check how many options are really left for the second place.
combi.wrongFix: The second digit can only be chosen in 2 ways, because the first digit cannot be used again. Correctly, 3 · 2 = {{total}} two-digit numbers can be made.
combi.orderIntro1: A few friends line up for a photo. In how many orders can they stand? Let us count systematically: first decide who stands at the front, then who comes next, and so on — by the end there is nothing left to choose.
combi.orderIntro2: With three friends the first place has 3 options, the second the remaining 2, the third only 1: 3 · 2 · 1 = 6 orders. This is the multiplication rule again, except every step has one option fewer.
combi.orderTreeAria: Tree of orders for {{n}} friends, with {{total}} orders.
combi.orderTooMany: {{total}} branches are too many to draw. The table shows how fast this number grows.
combi.orderDef: n factorial (n!): the product of the integers from 1 to n, n! = n · (n − 1) · … · 2 · 1. It is the number of ways n different things can be arranged in order. By convention 0! = 1.
combi.orderRule: n things can be arranged in order in n! ways. The table shows that ten people can already line up in more than three million ways.
combi.orderWordIntro: Let us rearrange the letters of the word {{word}}. If we could tell the two A's apart there would be {{all}} orders. But we cannot, so every word would appear on the list exactly twice: {{all}} has to be divided by 2.
combi.orderTask: Five friends sit down on a bench. {{first}} and {{second}} insist on sitting next to each other. How many seatings are possible?
combi.orderHint: Glue the two of them into a single block: then only 4 things have to be arranged. Inside the block the two of them can still swap places.
combi.ttIntro1: Monday has four lessons: maths, Hungarian, history and PE. With no conditions they make 4! = 24 timetables.
combi.ttIntro2: Switch conditions on and see how many are left. Branches of the tree die where a condition can no longer be met — the bad branches need not be drawn to the end.
combi.ttMathNotFirst: Maths is not the first lesson
combi.ttHuNextToHist: Hungarian and history are next to each other
combi.ttTreeAria: Tree of timetables, with {{total}} valid timetables.
combi.ttTooMany: That is too many branches to draw. Valid timetables: {{total}}.
combi.ttDead: The dashed, struck-out branches die exactly where the condition can no longer be met.
combi.ttNone: No timetable meets all of the conditions at once.
combi.ttSplit: This is case separation too: once one lesson is fixed, arranging the other three is a smaller, familiar problem. The big question is cut into a few small ones.
combi.ttTask: PE is the last lesson and maths is not the first. How many timetables are left?
combi.ttHint: Fix PE in the fourth slot: the other three can be placed in 3! = 6 ways. Subtract the ones that start with maths — there are 2 of those.
combi.selIntro1: We pick three of five classmates. If they form a team, the order we list them in makes no difference: Anna–Bence–Csilla is the same team as Csilla–Anna–Bence.
combi.selIntro2: But if we elect a president, a secretary and a treasurer, then a different order means different jobs, so there are more possibilities. Switch between the two views and see how much the number grows.
combi.selPickPrompt: Pick {{k}} people above and we will show you the orders they can stand in.
combi.selBridge: Every team of {{k}} can be lined up in {{each}} different orders, so with order there are exactly {{each}} times as many: {{teams}} · {{each}} = {{total}}.
combi.selDef: Variation (in English books: k-permutation): choosing k out of n things where the order matters. Combination: choosing k out of n things where the order does not matter. Every combination corresponds to k! variations.
combi.selNames: Instead of memorising the names, always ask the question: does the order matter? If yes, it is a variation; if not, a combination.
combi.selLottoTitle: How big is this number really?
combi.selLottoYears: Years at one ticket a week
combi.selLottoNote: That is how many ways 5 numbers can be chosen out of 90. Filling in a single ticket a week, this is how many years it would take to try them all.
combi.selTask: A team of 3 is put together from a club of 8 people. How many different teams are possible?
combi.selHint: There is no order inside a team. First work out the ordered count, 8 · 7 · 6, then divide it by 3! = 6.
combi.graphIntro1: Draw a few people as dots, and join two dots when the two people shook hands. That is all a graph is: it does not matter where the dots sit or whether the lines are straight, only what is joined to what.
combi.graphDef: Graph: a set of dots, the vertices, and lines joining some of them, the edges. The degree of a vertex is the number of edges that run into it.
combi.graphIntro2: The degree is shown in orange next to the vertex. Click two vertices one after the other and the edge between them appears or disappears; the buttons below the drawing do the same job.
combi.graphHandshake: The sum of the degrees is always twice the number of edges, however you draw the graph. Every edge has two ends, and it adds one to the degree at each of them.
combi.graphCompleteDef: Complete graph: a graph in which every pair of vertices is joined by exactly one edge.
combi.graphCompleteNote: If everyone shakes hands with everyone, every pair of vertices gets exactly one edge. So an edge is nothing but a choice of two vertices without order — exactly what we counted in the previous section.
combi.graphTask: There are 7 people at a party and everyone shakes hands with everyone else exactly once. How many handshakes are there?
combi.graphHint: Draw the complete graph on 7 vertices, or count like this: there are 7 · 6 handshake ends, but every handshake was counted twice.
combi.modelIntro1: Many word problems turn into a graph: people are the vertices and "they know each other" is an edge; or teams are the vertices and a match played is an edge. Once the graph is there, the question is usually only how many edges or how big a degree it has.
combi.modelPickD: How many others does everyone know?
combi.modelParityQuestion: Among {{n}} people everyone knows exactly {{d}} others. Is that possible?
combi.modelReason_ok: Yes, it is possible. The degrees would add up to {{sum}}, which means {{edges}} acquaintances, that is {{edges}} edges. One such graph is drawn below.
combi.modelReason_oddSum: Not possible. The degrees would add up to {{sum}}, which is odd — but the sum of the degrees is always twice the number of edges, so it is even.
combi.modelReason_degreeTooBig: Not possible. Nobody can know {{d}} others, because apart from themselves there are only {{n}} − 1 people.
combi.modelParityAria: Graph on {{n}} vertices where every vertex has degree {{d}}.
combi.modelParityNote: The graph we draw is only one of the possible answers: we seat the people in a circle and join everyone to those sitting nearest to them.
combi.modelStoryIntro: Four people and who knows whom. The degree is written next to each vertex.
combi.modelStoryAria: Graph on four vertices: Anna is joined to the other three, Bence and Csilla are joined to each other, Dani only to Anna.
combi.modelStoryTask: Which story describes this graph exactly?
combi.modelStoryHint: Count the edges running out of each person and compare them with the stories.
combi.storyStar: Anna knows everyone, Bence and Csilla know each other, and Dani knows only Anna.
combi.storyAll: All four of them know each other.
combi.storyTwoEach: Everyone knows exactly two other people.
combi.modelTask: 6 teams play a round robin: everyone plays everyone else exactly once. How many matches are there?
combi.modelHint: The same graph as the handshakes: every pair of teams gets one edge.
combi.sieveIntro1: We already met the sieve in the Sets lesson: adding the sizes of two sets counts the overlap twice, so it has to come off once. Now we do the same thing with numbers.
combi.sieveIntro2: The question: from 1 to 100, how many numbers are divisible by 2 or by 3? There are 50 multiples of 2 and 33 multiples of 3. But the multiples of 6 — the ones on both lists — were counted twice, so they come off once: 50 + 33 − 16 = 67.
combi.sieveGridAria: Grid of the numbers from 1 to {{limit}}, with the multiples of {{a}} and {{b}} coloured.
combi.sieveNames: Here A is the set of the multiples of {{a}} and B the set of the multiples of {{b}}.
combi.sieveNeitherNote: The numbers that are multiples of neither come from subtracting the coloured ones from all of them. It is the same idea as counting the bad cases and taking them away when that is the easier job.
combi.sieveTask: From 1 to 100, how many numbers are divisible by neither 3 nor 5?
combi.sieveHint: First count how many are divisible by 3 or by 5: 33 + 20 − 6. Then subtract that from 100.

num.towerTitle: 1. How the number sets are built on each other
num.towerIntro1: You learned to count with 1, 2, 3, … These are the natural numbers, and 0 belongs with them. But subtract 5 from 3 and you step out of them: you need −2 as well. Every new set of numbers is born this way — because some operation leads out of the old one.
num.towerIntro2: Click a number in the boxes. We show the narrowest set it belongs to. Watch out: the boxes are inside each other, so every natural number is an integer too, and every integer is rational too.
num.towerDef1: Natural numbers (ℕ): 0, 1, 2, 3, … — the counting numbers, with 0 included.
num.towerDef2: Integers (ℤ): the natural numbers and their opposites: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
num.towerDef3: Rational numbers (ℚ): the numbers that can be written as a quotient of two integers, in the form p/q with q ≠ 0. Their decimal form terminates or repeats.
num.towerDef4: Irrational numbers: the real numbers that cannot be written as a quotient of two integers. Their decimal form is endless and never repeats, for example √2 or π.
num.towerDef5: Real numbers (ℝ): the rational and the irrational numbers together. Every point of the number line is a real number, and every real number has its place on the line.
num.towerNone: Pick a number from the boxes and we will look at where it belongs.
num.towerSay_natural: This is a natural number: one of 0, 1, 2, 3, … So it is an integer and a rational number as well, since it can be written as a fraction, for example 7 = 7/1.
num.towerSay_integer: This is an integer but not a natural number, because it is negative. It is still rational, since it can be written as a fraction: −3 = −3/1.
num.towerSay_rational: This is a rational number: it can be written as one integer divided by another. It is not an integer, because on the number line it stands between two neighbouring whole numbers.
num.towerSay_irrational: This is an irrational number: no fraction p/q is equal to it. Its decimal form never stops and never falls into a repeating pattern.
num.towerWhyTitle: Why is a wider set always needed?
num.towerWhyZ: Subtraction leads out of the natural numbers. That is why the negative numbers are needed, and with them the integers, ℤ.
num.towerWhyQ: Division leads out of the integers. That is why fractions are needed, and with them the rationals, ℚ.
num.towerWhyR: Taking a root leads out of ℚ as well: no fraction squares to 2. That is why the real numbers, ℝ, are needed.
num.towerSetsLink: The ⊂ sign (subset) and the set operations are covered in detail in the Sets lesson.
num.towerTask: Which is the narrowest set of numbers the number belongs to? Choose in all five rows.
num.towerHint: Work out the roots first. If a number can be written as a fraction it is rational; if that fraction comes to a whole number it is an integer.
num.lawsTitle: 2. The laws of operations and the brackets
num.lawsIntro1: 3 · 4 or 4 · 3? The same thing. Turn a 3 × 4 rectangle and it becomes 4 × 3, but the number of little squares inside does not change. This is what being commutative means.
num.lawsIntro2: Drag the sliders and look at all three laws. Each says the same thing: the picture can be rearranged and the area stays. Addition and multiplication behave like this — subtraction and division do not.
num.lawsDef1: Commutativity: the order of the two terms does not matter. a + b = b + a and a · b = b · a.
num.lawsDef2: Associativity: the placing of the brackets does not matter. (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) and (a · b) · c = a · (b · c).
num.lawsDef3: Distributivity: a sum can be multiplied term by term. a · (b + c) = a · b + a · c.
num.lawsAria_comm: Two rectangles: one {{a}} × {{b}} and one {{b}} × {{a}}, with the same number of little squares.
num.lawsAria_assoc: {{a}} + {{b}} + {{c}} little squares in a row, marked up with two different groupings.
num.lawsAria_distrib: A rectangle {{a}} units wide, cut into a part {{b}} units tall and a part {{c}} units tall.
num.lawsRead_comm: Both rectangles hold the same number of squares: in a product the order does not matter.
num.lawsRead_assoc: The same row of {{a}} + {{b}} + {{c}}, grouped in two ways. Where the brackets go makes no difference, the sum is the same.
num.lawsRead_distrib: The rectangle was cut across. The two pieces have areas {{a}} · {{b}} and {{a}} · {{c}}, and together they are the whole rectangle.
num.lawsNotComm: Subtraction and division are not commutative: swap the two numbers and the result changes. Here the order matters very much.
num.lawsParenNote: Without brackets, multiplication and division come first and only then addition and subtraction. A bracket overrides this: whatever is inside has to be worked out first.
num.lawsCalcNote: A calculator follows exactly the same order. If it says something else than you expected, you probably left out a bracket.
num.lawsTask: Work out 47 · 99 in your head using the distributive law.
num.fracIntro1: 1/4 and 0.25 are the same number, just written differently. You can switch from one to the other any time: a fraction really is a division, and the decimal form is the result of that division.
num.fracIntro2: Pick a numerator and a denominator and watch the steps of the division. The remainder is the interesting part: once an earlier remainder comes back, everything repeats from there on.
num.fracDef: Terminating decimal: the decimal digits run out, for example 1/4 = 0.25. Repeating decimal: a group of digits, the period, repeats for ever, for example 4/11 = 0.3636… The period is marked with a bar over it.
num.fracRemainderNote: A remainder can only be 0, 1, …, {{q}} − 1, so there are finitely many of them. Within {{q}} steps it therefore either hits 0 or repeats an earlier remainder. So every fraction has a decimal form that either stops or repeats.
num.fracStopRule: The decimal stops exactly when the denominator of the reduced fraction is built from 2s and 5s only. Those are the divisors of 10, and the decimal form works with powers of 10.
num.fracBackTitle: Back again: from a decimal to a fraction
num.fracBackIntro: If the decimal stops it is easy: 0.75 = 75/100. If it repeats you need a trick — multiply it by a power of ten and subtract it from itself.
num.fracBackNote: Multiplying by 10 only shifts the point. After two shifts the two numbers have the very same tail, so subtracting wipes the endless tail out and leaves a whole number.
num.fracTask: Write the number 0.363636… as a common fraction. Give the numerator and the denominator in lowest terms.
num.lineTitle: 4. The real numbers on the number line
num.lineIntro1: On the number line every real number has exactly one place, and every place holds exactly one number. Pick a number and we will show you where.
num.lineIntro2: A rational number’s decimal form either stops or repeats; an irrational one’s never settles. Their places are just as exact all the same: √2 is not “roughly” somewhere, it is at one definite point.
num.lineAria: Number line from −3 to 4, with {{name}} selected.
num.lineNoteRational: This is a rational number, so its decimal form stops or repeats: you can write it down exactly.
num.lineNoteIrrational: This is an irrational number. However many decimals you write down it is still only an approximation — but its place on the line is exact.
num.lineSqrtIntro: Stand a square of side 1 on the segment from 0 to 1. By Pythagoras its diagonal is √2 long. With a pair of compasses you can lay that length onto the number line.
num.lineSqrtAria: A unit square on the segment from 0 to 1, its diagonal swung onto the number line with an arc.
num.lineSqrtNote: No fraction writes this length down exactly, yet there it is on the line — a pair of compasses and a ruler find it. So irrational numbers are not something vague: they are points just as real as the rest.
num.lineZoomIntro: Pick a number and step further in. Each step cuts the interval into ten equal parts and asks which one the number falls into. The number of that part is exactly its next decimal digit.
num.lineZoomPickAria: Which number to zoom in on
num.lineZoomAria: The number line zoomed to {{level}} decimals, with {{name}} marked.
num.lineZoomNote_root2: The decimals of √2: {{digits}}… They never stop and never start repeating. That is the mark of an irrational number.
num.lineZoomNote_pi: The decimals of π: {{digits}}… Trillions of them have been worked out and nobody has found a pattern — nor will they, because π is irrational.
num.lineZoomNote_third: The decimals of 1/3: {{digits}}… The same 3 keeps coming. It is rational, and its period is a single digit long.
num.lineZoomNote_twentyTwoSevenths: The decimals of 22/7: {{digits}}… The block 142857 repeats for ever. This number is an old approximation of π, but it is not π: they part company at the third decimal.
num.lineTask: Which two neighbouring tenths does √10 fall between? Choose the lower one.
num.lineHint: Square them: 3.1² = 9.61, which is less than 10; 3.2² = 10.24, which is already more.
num.intervalIntro1: When we say "the numbers between 2 and 5", one question is always left open: do 2 and 5 themselves belong? Interval notation answers exactly that.
num.intervalIntro2: A filled circle: the endpoint is included, that end is closed. An empty circle: the endpoint is left out, that end is open. Switch the ends around and see what changes.
num.intervalDef1: Interval: one connected piece of the number line: the set of numbers lying between two endpoints.
num.intervalDef2: Closed interval [a, b]: both endpoints belong to it, that is a ≤ x ≤ b. Open interval (a, b): neither endpoint belongs, that is a < x < b. A half-open interval closes one end and opens the other.
num.intervalAria: An interval from {{from}} to {{to}}, its left end {{left}} and its right end {{right}}.
num.intWhyInside: It lies between the two endpoints.
num.intWhyLeftClosed: This is the left endpoint, and the left end is closed, so it is included.
num.intWhyLeftOpen: This is the left endpoint, but the left end is open, so it is left out.
num.intWhyRightClosed: This is the right endpoint, and the right end is closed, so it is included.
num.intWhyRightOpen: This is the right endpoint, but the right end is open, so it is left out.
num.intWhyBelow: It is smaller than the left endpoint.
num.intWhyAbove: It is bigger than the right endpoint.
num.intervalOtherNote: Hungarian textbooks turn the bracket outwards at an open end: what we write as (a, b) they write as ]a; b[. In a foreign textbook, always check which notation is in use.
num.intervalTask: Which interval is the set of the numbers x for which −1 < x ≤ 3?
num.intervalHint: Strictly greater than −1: −1 is left out, so the left end is open. Less than or equal to 3: 3 is included, so the right end is closed.
num.absIntro1: Three simple things you can do to a number: mirror it across 0, ask how far it is from 0, and find the partner that multiplies with it to give 1.
num.absDef1: Opposite (−x): the number that is as far from 0 as x, on the other side. The two add up to 0.
num.absDef2: Absolute value (|x|): the distance of the number from 0 on the number line. It is never negative.
num.absDef3: Reciprocal (1/x): the number that multiplied by x gives 1. Zero has no reciprocal.
num.absIntro2: Drag the slider and watch the three points. The opposite is always mirrored in 0. The farther a number is from 0, the closer its reciprocal sits to 0 — and 0 has no reciprocal at all.
num.absAria: Number line: x = {{x}}, its opposite {{opposite}}, and its reciprocal are all marked.
num.absFact1: A number and its opposite always add up to 0.
num.absFact2: A number times its reciprocal is always 1. That is why 0 has no reciprocal: multiplying by 0 never gives 1.
num.absFact3: An absolute value is never negative, and a number and its opposite have the same absolute value.
num.absFact4: The reciprocal of a fraction is that fraction turned upside down. So a number between 0 and 1 has a reciprocal bigger than 1.
num.absFact5: The absolute value of a difference is the distance of the two numbers on the line.
num.absTask: What is the opposite of the reciprocal of −3/4? Give the numerator and the denominator.
num.absHint: The reciprocal of −3/4 is that fraction turned over, so −4/3. Its opposite is the same number with the sign swapped.
num.estIntro1: Roughly how much is 398 · 51? Round both numbers to a single leading digit: 400 · 50 = 20 000. If the machine says 2 030, you mistyped something.
num.estIntro2: Estimating does not replace working it out, it comes before it. Once you know roughly how big the answer will be, a wrong keypress jumps out at you.
num.estDef1: Estimate: a quick approximation of the size of a result, done in your head with rounded numbers.
num.estDef2: Significant digit: the digits of a number starting from the first non-zero one. The first significant digit of 398 is 3; rounded to one significant digit it is 400.
num.estOff: The estimate is about {{percent}}% away from the exact value. That is plenty for checking how big the answer should be.
num.estRule: Estimate first, calculate second. If the machine says something else than you expected, check what you typed before you doubt the maths.
num.targetIntro: Use the digits {{digits}}, each of them exactly once, with the signs + − · : and brackets. Can you reach the target?
num.targetBadChars: Only digits, the signs + − · : and brackets may be used.
num.targetBadDigits: Each of the four digits ({{digits}}) has to be used exactly once.
num.targetBadExpr: I cannot work this one out. Check the brackets and the operation signs.
num.targetValue: The expression comes to {{value}}. Keep trying!
num.estTask: Five results somebody got with a calculator. Which are plausible and which are certainly wrong? Decide in your head, by estimating.
num.estHint: Round every number to one leading digit and work it out in your head. Watch the size: 612 : 3 is roughly 600 : 3 = 200.
num.roundIntro1: Rounding means throwing away the digits you do not need so that the number changes as little as possible. A single digit always decides whether it goes down or up.
num.roundIntro2: Pick a number and a place. The digits you keep stay in solid boxes, the deciding digit is highlighted and the dropped ones get a dashed box.
num.roundDef: Rounding: replacing a number by the nearest number that stops at a chosen place value. The first digit after the kept ones decides: 0 to 4 rounds down, 5 to 9 rounds up.
num.roundRule: 0–4 down, 5–9 up. The digits behind the deciding one no longer matter: even the ones after a 5 do not change the decision.
num.measureTitle: Measuring: how far can you trust the digits?
num.measureIntro: You measure the floor of the room: {{length}} m long and {{width}} m wide. Their product has plenty of decimals, but the tape was not that precise. Choose a measuring error.
num.measureDef: Measurement error: the possible gap between the measured value and the true value. If the tape is accurate to ±5 mm, the true length may differ from the reading by at most 5 mm in either direction.
num.measureSure: Only these digits are certain: {{sure}} m². The rest of {{nominal}} m² only looks precise — the measurement does not support it.
num.measureNote: A result can never be more precise than the measurement it came from. That is why rounding makes sense: the extra digits do not show knowledge, they hide what you do not know.
num.roundHint: The digit after the thousandths place is 5, so it rounds up.

deriv.title: The derivative: a secant becoming a tangent
deriv.intro1: The derivative answers one question: how steep is the curve at a single point x₀? Think of the curve as a hill you are walking on — the derivative is the slope of the ground exactly under your feet.
deriv.intro2: There's a problem, though. Slope means "rise over run", and that needs two points. One point has no rise and no run. So we cheat in three steps:
deriv.steps12: 1. Pick a second point a small distance h away, at x₀+h. 2. Draw the straight line through both points — the orange secant — and measure its slope, which is just rise over run:
deriv.step3: 3. Shrink h. As the second point slides toward the first, the secant tips over into the dashed tangent — the line that just grazes the curve. The derivative is defined as the value this slope settles on:
deriv.dragNote: Drag the h slider toward 0 and watch it happen. The numbers under the chart update live with your slider.
deriv.texLimitHeading: the limit it is heading for:
deriv.noTangent: No tangent here! Coming from the right the slopes settle on {{right}}, but coming from the left they settle on {{left}}. The two sides disagree, so there is no single answer and f′({{x0}}) does not exist. The curve has a corner at this point.
deriv.tableTitle: The limit, computed like a math student
deriv.tableIntro: "Limit as h approaches 0" sounds abstract, but you can't actually set h = 0 — that would divide by zero. A limit is a promise instead: the closer h gets to 0, the closer the slope gets to one particular number. On paper that promise is just a table. Halve h again and again and watch the right-hand column stop changing. The number it settles on is the derivative.
deriv.tryIt: Try it: pick |x| and slide x₀ to 0. The table refuses to settle, because approaching from the right gives +1 and from the left gives −1 (tick the checkbox to compare the two directions). A corner has no single steepness — that is exactly what "the limit does not exist" means. Then try sin(x) at x₀ = 0 and watch the quotients march to exactly 1: the sine curve leaves the origin at 45°.
deriv.chartAria: Function with secant and tangent lines

integ.title: The integral: rectangles becoming area
integ.intro1: The integral answers: how much area sits between the curve and the x-axis, from a to b? For a rectangle that's easy — width times height. But a curved roof has no ready-made area formula. So, just like with the derivative, we cheat with straight edges, in three steps:
integ.step1: 1. Cut the stretch from a to b into n equal strips. Each strip has width
integ.step2: 2. On each strip, stand a rectangle. Its height is the curve's value at one chosen spot in the strip (the left edge, the middle, or the right edge — your choice above). Rectangles we can measure: each one contributes height × width, and adding all n of them gives the Riemann sum:
integ.step3: 3. Use more, thinner strips. The error lives in the little slivers between the flat rectangle tops and the curve, and thinner strips leave smaller slivers. The integral is the value the total settles on — and the ∫ symbol is literally a stretched-out S, for "sum":
integ.dragNote: Drag n up and watch the orange rectangles melt into the blue area. The numbers under the chart track your sliders.
integ.texLimitHeading: the limit it is heading for:
integ.degenerate: a and b coincide — the area of a zero-width region is 0. Drag them apart.
integ.tableTitle: The limit again, as a table
integ.tableIntro: Same move as on the Derivative tab: a limit is a promise that the numbers settle, and a table makes the promise visible. Each row doubles the number of rectangles. Read down the third column and watch it stop changing — the value it locks onto is the integral.
integ.tryIt: Try it: switch "left edge" to "midpoint" and watch the table settle dramatically faster. Sampling in the middle of each strip lets the rectangle's overshoot on one side cancel its undershoot on the other. Integrate sin(x) from −2 to 2 and get 0: area below the axis counts as negative, and the two halves cancel exactly. And try |x| — the corner that broke the derivative gives the integral no trouble at all, because adding areas doesn't care about a kink the way slopes do. That one-sidedness is why the fundamental theorem of calculus — the statement that derivative and integral undo each other — is a real theorem someone had to prove, not an obvious fact.
integ.chartAria: Function with true area shaded and Riemann rectangles

fft.subtitle: The Fourier transform's claim: any repeating signal is secretly a sum of simple waves. This page lets you test the claim. Type a function, and the app measures it at N points, finds which waves hide inside (the FFT), throws away all but the strongest ones, and rebuilds the signal from what's left (the inverse FFT). If the rebuilt curve still matches, a few waves were enough to carry the whole signal.
fft.keepLabel: Strongest components to keep (zero-amplitude bins are skipped): {{n}}
fft.timeNote: The blue curve is your function, measured at N points. The dashed orange curve is the rebuilt version — the inverse FFT of only the kept components. Where the two hug each other, those few waves already tell the whole story; drag the "components" slider down and watch the orange curve lose detail first, then shape.
fft.waveNote: Here are the hidden waves the FFT found, drawn one per row so you can see each ingredient on its own — strongest first, all on the same y-scale so heights are comparable. Each label gives the wave's recipe: strength × cos(speed × x + head start). Add every row together, point by point, and you get exactly the dashed orange curve above.
fft.freqNote: The same information as a bar chart — the signal's "recipe card". One bar per possible frequency (bin k = 0 … N/2): its position says how fast that wave repeats, its height says how strongly it is present. Most bars are near zero because most frequencies simply aren't in the signal. Hover a bar for its exact frequency, amplitude and phase; click one to see its value computed step by step below.
fft.binNote: Pick a bin with the +/− buttons, or click any bar in the spectrum above, and watch its value worked out by hand.
fft.resultNote: The recipe in one line — this sum of simple waves is what the inverse FFT actually draws as the dashed curve. The RMS error above says how far that drawing is from your function, averaged over all sample points (0 means a perfect match).

bin.picker: bin k = {{k}} · the wave with {{k}} cycles per window (f = {{f}})
bin.intro: A "bin" is one slot of the transform's output. Bin k asks a single question: how much of the signal is a wave that repeats exactly {{k}} times across the window? To answer it, the DFT compares the signal against that wave, sample by sample: multiply them together and add everything up. Where the signal moves in step with the reference wave the products pile up; where it doesn't, they cancel. The whole definition is one line (the e-power is just shorthand for a cosine and sine pair):
bin.plugged: With this bin's numbers plugged in:
bin.rowsTitle: One row per sample — first {{shown}} of {{n}} rows:
bin.assemble: Now assemble the answer from the two column totals. The cosine total becomes the real part, the sine total (with its sign flipped, from the −i in the definition) becomes the imaginary part:
bin.strength: Those two numbers hold the wave's strength and its shift. The strength (amplitude) is the length of the pair, read off with Pythagoras{{doubled}}:
bin.strengthDoubled: , doubled because a real signal splits its energy between this bin and its mirror twin
bin.phaseIntro: The shift (phase) is the pair's angle:
bin.contribIntro: So this bin contributes one wave to the signal:
bin.detailsSummary: Why the sums single out this frequency (graphical view)
bin.colProd: 2 · their product — the shaded area is what gets summed
bin.whyNote: If the signal contains this frequency it stays in step with the reference, the products pile up on one side of zero, and the sum is large. Any other frequency drifts in and out of step, so the shaded area cancels toward 0.

alias.title: Aliasing: when sampling lies
alias.intro: Everything above rests on one quiet assumption: that N samples are enough to know which wave produced them. This demo is where the assumption breaks. A computer cannot store a smooth curve, only samples of it — here a sine with a frequency you control, sampled at the same 64 evenly spaced points (green dots) no matter how fast it oscillates. To capture a wiggle you need at least 2 samples per cycle: one near a crest, one near a trough. With 64 samples that caps honest measurement at 32 cycles per window. Push beyond it and the samples do not go blank — they lie.
alias.sliderLabel: True frequency: {{k}} cycles per window (Nyquist limit is 32)
alias.verdictNyquist: {{k}} cycles is exactly N/2. A sine at this frequency crosses zero at every single sample point — all 64 measurements read 0, and the wave vanishes without a trace.
alias.verdictFaithful: {{k}} cycles stays at or below N/2 = 32, so every cycle gets at least 2 samples. The measurements describe the wave truthfully, and the energy lands in bin {{bin}}. The two curves are one and the same.
alias.turnsClause_one: {{count}} whole turn between consecutive samples is invisible, and
alias.turnsClause_other: {{count}} whole turns between consecutive samples are invisible, and
alias.verdictFlippedA: what's left over looks like {{bin}} cycles running backwards. The measurements are identical to
alias.verdictFlippedB: , so the energy lands in bin {{bin}}.
alias.verdictWrapped_one: the {{count}} whole turn between consecutive samples is invisible, so the measurements are identical to a {{bin}}-cycle wave. The energy lands in bin {{bin}}.
alias.verdictWrapped_other: the {{count}} whole turns between consecutive samples are invisible, so the measurements are identical to a {{bin}}-cycle wave. The energy lands in bin {{bin}}.
alias.wholeTitle: The whole window — every green dot is an overlap point where the two curves cross, and the dots are all the computer ever sees
alias.zoomTitle: Zoomed to x = 0 … ⅛ — watch {{trueF}} thread through the same overlap points that {{other}} passes through
alias.foldTitle: The folding map — where every true frequency ends up
alias.foldNote: Frequencies fold back and forth like an accordion: up to Nyquist they map to themselves, from 32 to 64 they come back mirrored, past 64 the pattern repeats. The marker is the slider's current position.
alias.whyNote: Why this matters. Between the dots the two curves disagree completely, but sampling never looks between the dots, so no algorithm can recover which wave was real: the evidence is destroyed at the moment of sampling, not by the FFT. That has a physical picture — film a wheel spinning 60 times a second with a 64-frames-per-second camera and it appears to roll slowly backwards, which is why helicopter rotors do impossible things on video. It also has an engineering consequence: since no computation can undo aliasing, real systems prevent it before sampling, with an analog filter that deletes everything above Nyquist. That is why 44.1 kHz audio can only represent tones up to about 22 kHz, and why every analog-to-digital converter ships with an anti-aliasing filter in front of it.
alias.tryIt: Try it: drag to 4 (faithful — the curves coincide), 31 (barely legal, 2 samples per cycle), 32 (a Nyquist sine vanishes), 60 (the classic: reads as 4 backwards), 64 (one full turn per step — looks like standing still, bin 0), and 92 (wraps past N and reads as 28 backwards).
